title:
RETRACTED ARTICLE: Fatal factitious Cushing
syndrome (Münchhausen’s syndrome) in a patient with macroprolactinoma and silent
corticotrophinoma: case report and literature review
case_prompt:
A 26-year-old woman, a former health professional with a history of treated depression and a prolactin-secreting pituitary macroadenoma managed by transsphenoidal surgery in 2010 (with normalization of prolactin and no glucocorticoid replacement), presented in 2013 with episodic features of Cushing syndrome, including weight gain, new-onset hypertension, and diabetes.  
Laboratory evaluation using chemiluminescence immunoassay showed a 24-hour urinary total cortisol of 12 200 μg/24 h (normal 50–310 μg/24 h) but a normal morning serum cortisol of 12 μg/dL (normal 5–25 μg/dL). Midnight salivary cortisol by ELISA was elevated above the normal range. Plasma ACTH was 14 pg/mL (normal 10–46 pg/mL), and serum DHEA-S was low at 208 ng/mL (normal 988–3400 ng/mL). Abdominal CT revealed normal adrenal glands. A pituitary MRI showed a 1–2 cm cystic lesion in the sella, described as similar to her prior tumor but also possibly an arachnoid cyst. The patient denied any use of exogenous glucocorticoids.  
What is the most likely diagnosis?
diagnostic_reasoning: 1. Cyclic Cushing syndrome was considered because of the intermittent hypercortisolism — “four years later, the patient presented with typical, albeit sporadic, signs and symptoms of Cushing syndrome… indicating potential cyclic CS.” 2. Recurrent pituitary corticotropinoma was considered given the pituitary MRI finding — “pituitary MRI exhibited a cystic lesion similar to the previous tumor tissue, but could also represent an arachnoid cyst.” 3. Factitious glucocorticoid use (factitious Cushing syndrome) was considered despite patient denial — “Exogenous intake of glucocorticoids was strongly denied by the patient.” 4. Endogenous ACTH–dependent Cushing syndrome was questioned because DHEA-S was suppressed, whereas “ACTH-dependent CS is associated with normal/high levels of this hormone. In our case… DHEA-S levels were suppressed.”
